feedbacks: Using the -reconfigure flag with the terraform init command allows you to reconfigure the backend without copying the existing state. This is the correct flag to use when changing the backend configuration without transferring the existing state data.

The -migrate-state flag is not the correct option in this scenario. This flag is used for migrating state data from one backend to another, rather than simply reconfiguring the backend without copying the existing state.

The -backend=false flag is not the appropriate choice for reconfiguring the backend without copying the existing state. This flag disables the backend configuration entirely, which is not the desired outcome in this situation.

This answer is incorrect because -force-copy does the opposite of what is required. It is a real terraform init flag, but it suppresses the migration prompt and answers yes, forcing Terraform to copy (migrate) the existing state into the new backend. Since the goal is to reconfigure without copying state, -reconfigure is the correct flag."

question: A resource was changed manually outside of Terraform. You don't want to make any changes yet, but you want to see how the state would be updated to match the current real-world values. Which command should you run?
questionPlain: A resource was changed manually outside of Terraform. You don't want to make any changes yet, but you want to see how the state would be updated to match the current real-world values. Which command should you run?

choices.text: terraform plan -refresh-only
terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform state pull
terraform validate

explanation:
Objective 6d - Manage resource drift and Terraform state

Refresh-only mode: creates a plan whose goal is only to update the Terraform state and any root module output values to match changes made to remote objects outside of Terraform. This can be useful if you've intentionally changed one or more remote objects outside of the usual workflow (e.g., while responding to an incident) and you now need to reconcile Terraform's records with those changes.

Activate refresh-only mode using the -refresh-only command line option.
feedbacks: Running terraform plan -refresh-only will show you how the state would be updated to match the current real-world values without making any changes to the infrastructure. This command will refresh the state of the resources without applying any changes.

terraform apply -refresh-only updates the state file (and can write changes), which the question explicitly wants to avoid. We only want to see what would change, so plan -refresh-only is the better choice.

Running terraform state pull will retrieve the current state data from the Terraform state file, but it will not show you how the state would be updated to match the current real-world values after a manual change outside of Terraform.

Running terraform validate will check the configuration files for syntax errors and other issues, but it will not show you how the state would be updated to match the current real-world values after a manual change outside of Terraform.

question: In Terraform, what does “drift” mean in the context of a workspace’s state?
questionPlain: In Terraform, what does “drift” mean in the context of a workspace’s state?

choices.text: Real infrastructure has changed outside Terraform and no longer matches the desired state.
The configuration files were refactored and now use different argument ordering.
Provider versions were upgraded but no resources or state values changed at all.
The backend was migrated, but the state contents remained exactly the same.

explanation:
Objective 6d - Manage resource drift and Terraform state

One challenge when managing infrastructure as code is drift. Drift is the term for when the real-world state of your infrastructure differs from the state defined in your configuration. This can happen for many reasons. Within the context of your configuration, it happens when adding or removing resources or changing resource definitions. External to your configuration, drift occurs when resources are terminated or fail, or when changes are made manually or via other automation tools.
feedbacks: "Drift" in the context of a workspace's state in Terraform refers to the scenario where the actual infrastructure has been modified outside of Terraform, causing it to deviate from the desired state defined in the configuration. This can lead to inconsistencies and potential issues in managing the infrastructure.

Refactoring configuration files with different argument ordering does not relate to the concept of "drift" in Terraform. Drift specifically refers to changes in the actual infrastructure that are not reflected in the Terraform state.

Upgrading provider versions without any changes to resources or state values does not constitute "drift" in Terraform. Drift specifically refers to discrepancies between the desired state and the actual state of the infrastructure.

Migrating the backend while keeping the state contents the same does not result in "drift" in Terraform. Drift occurs when the actual infrastructure changes outside of Terraform's control, leading to inconsistencies between the desired and actual states.

question: You deployed resources using the CLI, but want to start managing them with Terraform moving forward. What steps are required to start managing resources with Terraform without impacting the resources themselves? (select three)
questionPlain: You deployed resources using the CLI, but want to start managing them with Terraform moving forward. What steps are required to start managing resources with Terraform without impacting the resources themselves? (select three)

choices.text: write Terraform resource blocks that match the existing settings
add import blocks mapping each address to its real ID
run terraform apply to import them in state with no changes
run terraform apply to recreate all resources from Terraform
define data sources for all of the existing resources

explanation:
Objective 7a - Import existing infrastructure into your Terraform workspace

To adopt existing infrastructure, you must have matching resource blocks in code and use imports (import blocks or terraform import) to map real objects into Terraform state. This records them without recreating or modifying the resources; afterward, Terraform manages drift and future changes.
feedbacks: Writing Terraform resource blocks that match the existing settings is necessary to define the resources in Terraform configuration. This step ensures that Terraform can manage the resources without changing their current settings.

Adding import blocks mapping each address to its real ID is essential to link the existing resources to their corresponding Terraform configuration. This step allows Terraform to recognize and manage the resources without recreating them.

Running terraform apply to import the resources in state with no changes is crucial to bring the existing resources under Terraform's management without modifying their configurations. This step ensures that Terraform can effectively track and manage resources.

Running terraform apply to recreate all resources from Terraform is not the correct approach in this scenario. The goal is to start managing existing resources with Terraform without impacting them, not to recreate them from scratch.

Defining data sources for all of the existing resources is not necessary in this case. Data sources are used to fetch information from external sources, not to manage existing resources that are already deployed.

question: Some of your production resources were created manually in the Azure portal. The company requires all production resources to be managed through Terraform. What should you do to bring those existing resources under Terraform management without disrupting them?
questionPlain: Some of your production resources were created manually in the Azure portal. The company requires all production resources to be managed through Terraform. What should you do to bring those existing resources under Terraform management without disrupting them?

choices.text: Use the import block to import the existing resources under Terraform management.
Rewrite the Terraform configuration file to deploy new resources, run a terraform apply, and migrate users to the newly deployed resources. Manually delete the other resources.
Run a terraform get to retrieve other resources that are not under Terraform management.
resources created outside of Terraform cannot be managed by Terraform

explanation:
Objective 7a - Import existing infrastructure into your Terraform workspace

To import manually created resources into Terraform without affecting the availability of the deployed resources, follow these steps:


  1. Import the existing resources: You can use the import block to import the existing resources into Terraform.


  2. Modify the Terraform configuration: Modify the Terraform configuration to reflect the desired state of the resources. This will allow you to manage the resources using Terraform just like any other Terraform-managed resource


  3. Test the changes: Before applying the changes, you can use the terraform plan command to preview the changes that will be made to the resources. This will allow you to verify that the changes will not negatively impact the availability of the resources.


  4. Apply the changes: If the changes are correct, you can use the terraform apply command to officially import the resources and pull them under Terraform management

By following these steps, you can start managing manually created resources in Terraform without impacting the availability of the deployed resources.
feedbacks: Using the import block allows you to bring existing resources under Terraform management without disrupting them. This method enables you to map the existing resources to Terraform configuration and state files, ensuring that Terraform can manage them effectively without recreating or deleting them.

Rewriting the Terraform configuration file to deploy new resources and manually deleting existing resources is not the recommended approach for bringing existing resources under Terraform management. This method can lead to disruptions in the production environment and may cause downtime or data loss.

Running terraform get retrieves modules from remote repositories to be used in the Terraform configuration. However, it does not bring existing resources under Terraform management. This command is used to download modules, not to manage existing resources created outside of Terraform.

It is incorrect to say that resources created outside of Terraform cannot be managed by Terraform. Terraform provides the ability to import existing resources into its state and configuration files using an import block in the configuration file. This allows management of existing resources without manual intervention or recreation.

question: A colleague asks what the difference is between terraform show and terraform state show. What is the correct explanation? (select three)
questionPlain: A colleague asks what the difference is between terraform show and terraform state show. What is the correct explanation? (select three)

choices.text: terraform show displays the entire state file without requiring any additional arguments
terraform state show requires you to specify a resource address to view that specific resource
terraform show is useful when you want a complete overview of all managed infrastructure
terraform state show can display multiple resources by separating them with commas
terraform show only displays resources that have pending changes
terraform state show automatically formats its output as JSON for machine parsing

explanation:
Objective 7b - Use the CLI to inspect state

The key differences between these commands relate to scope and usage. The terraform show command displays the complete contents of the state file in human-readable format without requiring any arguments, making it ideal for getting a full overview of your infrastructure. In contrast, terraform state show is targeted and requires a specific resource address as an argument, such as terraform state show aws_instance.web, to view details about just that resource.
feedbacks: terraform show is a command that displays the entire state file, including all resources and their current configuration, without the need for any additional arguments. It provides a high-level overview of the managed infrastructure.

When using terraform state show, you need to specify a resource address to view the details of that specific resource. This command allows you to inspect the state of individual resources within the Terraform state.

terraform show is particularly useful when you want to have a comprehensive overview of all the managed infrastructure in your Terraform configuration. It allows you to see the current state of all resources at once.
terraform state show does not have the capability to display multiple resources by separating them with commas. It is designed to show the state of a single resource specified by its address.
terraform show does not only display resources that have pending changes. It shows the current state of all resources in the Terraform configuration, regardless of whether there are pending changes.

terraform state show does not automatically format its output as JSON for machine parsing. The output format is human-readable and provides detailed information about the state of a specific resource within the Terraform state.

question: What environment variable can be set to enable detailed logging for Terraform?
questionPlain: What environment variable can be set to enable detailed logging for Terraform?

choices.text: TF_LOG
TF_DEBUG
TF_TRACE
TF_INFO

explanation:
Objective 7c - Describe when and how to use verbose logging

Terraform has detailed logs that can be enabled by setting the TF_LOG environment variable to any value. This will cause detailed logs to appear on stderr.

You can set TF_LOG to one of the log levels TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR to change the verbosity of the logs. TRACE is the most verbose and it is the default if TF_LOG is set to something other than a log level name.

https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/debugging
feedbacks: The TF_LOG environment variable can be set to enable detailed logging for Terraform. It allows users to see more detailed information about the actions Terraform is taking, which can be helpful for troubleshooting and understanding the execution flow.
Terraform does not use a TF_DEBUG environment variable for logging. Detailed logs are enabled with TF_LOG.
Terraform does not define a TF_TRACE environment variable. Logging verbosity is controlled with TF_LOG (and optionally TF_LOG_PATH), not TF_TRACE.
Terraform does not use a TF_INFO environment variable for logging. Detailed logs are enabled with TF_LOG.

question: You are using an HCP Terraform workflow that is connected to a VCS repository (VCS-driven workflow) and want to deploy a new resource. Which sequence of steps follows the recommended workflow?
questionPlain: You are using an HCP Terraform workflow that is connected to a VCS repository (VCS-driven workflow) and want to deploy a new resource. Which sequence of steps follows the recommended workflow?

choices.text:
1. Add the new resource block to the Terraform configuration in the repo

2. Open a pull request with the change

3. After the plan is generated, approve the apply in HCP Terraform

1. Write the new resource block in the HCP Terraform UI

2. Manually start a new run with “Queue plan”

3. Approve the apply when it completes

1. Add the new resource block locally and run terraform apply on your laptop

2. Push the updated terraform.tfstate file to the repo

3. Skip review so HCP Terraform doesn’t re-run the plan

1. Commit the new resource block directly to the main branch

2. Disable policy checks to allow the apply to run automatically

3. Re-enable policies after the resource is created

explanation:
Objective 8a - Use HCP Terraform to create infrastructure

In an HCP Terraform VCS-driven workflow, your Terraform configuration lives in version control, not in the UI. To add new infrastructure, you update the code (for example, by adding a new resource block), open a pull request, and let HCP Terraform automatically create a run and show you the plan for that change. After review/approval, you authorize the apply in HCP Terraform.

This gives you change history, review controls, policy checks, and auditable applies instead of people running terraform apply on their laptops.
feedbacks: This sequence follows the recommended VCS-driven workflow for deploying a new resource using HCP Terraform. By adding the new resource block to the Terraform configuration in the repository, opening a pull request with the change, and then approving the apply after the plan is generated, you ensure that the deployment process is controlled, reviewed, and tracked effectively.

Writing the new resource block directly in the HCP Terraform UI and manually starting a new run with "Queue plan" bypasses the version control and review process provided by VCS-driven workflows. This approach may lead to inconsistencies, lack of visibility, and potential errors in the deployment process.

Adding the new resource block locally and running terraform apply on your laptop, then pushing the updated terraform.tfstate file to the repository, and skipping the review in HCP Terraform can introduce discrepancies between the local environment and the repository, potentially causing issues with version control and collaboration.

Committing the new resource block directly to the main branch, disabling policy checks to allow automatic apply, and then re-enabling policies after the resource is created, bypasses the recommended review and approval process. This approach can lead to uncontrolled changes, potential conflicts, and lack of visibility into the deployment process.

question: Your team uses HCP Terraform with a CLI-driven workflow. After making changes to your configuration locally, you run terraform plan. Where does the plan operation execute?
questionPlain: Your team uses HCP Terraform with a CLI-driven workflow. After making changes to your configuration locally, you run terraform plan. Where does the plan operation execute?

choices.text: on HCP Terraform infrastructure with results streamed back to your terminal
locally on your machine, then the results are uploaded to HCP Terraform for storage
on a self-hosted agent that you must configure in your workspace settings
on your local machine with no interaction with HCP Terraform infrastructure

explanation:
Objective 8a - Use HCP Terraform to create infrastructure

In a CLI-driven workflow with HCP Terraform, plan and apply operations execute remotely on HCP Terraform's infrastructure by default, not on your local machine. This is called remote operations. When you run terraform plan or terraform apply, your configuration files are uploaded to HCP Terraform, the operation runs there, and the output is streamed back to your terminal in real-time. This ensures consistent execution environments, enables better collaboration, and supports features such as policy checks and cost estimation.
feedbacks: When you run the terraform plan command in a CLI-driven workflow with HCP Terraform, the plan operation is executed on the HCP Terraform infrastructure. The results of the plan are then streamed back to your terminal for review and analysis, allowing you to see the planned changes and potential impacts directly from the HCP Terraform environment.

The plan operation in HCP Terraform does not execute locally on your machine and then upload the results to the platform for storage. Instead, the plan is executed directly on the HCP Terraform infrastructure to ensure consistency and accuracy in the planning process. Uploading results from a local machine would introduce potential discrepancies and security risks.

HCP Terraform does not require users to configure self-hosted agents for executing plan operations. The platform handles the execution of terraform plan directly on its infrastructure, eliminating the need for additional configuration or setup on self-hosted agents. This ensures a streamlined and efficient workflow for users.

In a CLI-driven workflow with HCP Terraform, the plan operation is not executed solely on your local machine without any interaction with the HCP Terraform infrastructure. The platform plays a crucial role in executing the plan operation to provide accurate insights into the planned changes and their potential impact, ensuring a consistent and reliable planning process.

question: Which feature of HCP Terraform enables you to publish and maintain a set of custom modules that can only be used within your organization?
questionPlain: Which feature of HCP Terraform enables you to publish and maintain a set of custom modules that can only be used within your organization?

choices.text: HCP Terraform private registry
the public Terraform Registry
a custom VCS integration to your repo
HCP Terraform agents

explanation:
Objective 8b - Describe HCP Terraform collaboration and governance features

You can use modules from a private registry, like the one provided by HCP Terraform. Private registry modules use source strings in the form of a specific format. This format is the same as the public registry's but adds a hostname prefix.
feedbacks: The HCP Terraform private registry allows you to publish and maintain a set of custom modules that are only accessible within your organization. This ensures that your organization's specific modules are securely stored and can only be used by authorized users within your organization.

The public Terraform Registry is a repository of publicly available Terraform modules that can be accessed by anyone. It does not provide the level of privacy and control needed to restrict module usage to only within your organization.

While a custom VCS integration to your repo can help manage your Terraform code, it does not provide the specific feature of enabling you to publish and maintain custom modules that are restricted to use within your organization.

HCP Terraform agents are responsible for executing Terraform runs in the HCP environment and do not have the functionality to enable the publishing and maintenance of custom modules for internal use within your organization.

question: In HCP Terraform, what is the purpose of using a run trigger?
questionPlain: In HCP Terraform, what is the purpose of using a run trigger?

choices.text: to automatically queue a new run in one workspace after another workspace applies successfully
to provide temporary cloud credentials so a workspace can authenticate with least privilege during runs
to force a workspace to always run from the newest commit of its VCS branch
to require human approval before applying changes in specific workspaces, such as production environments

explanation:
Objective 8c - Describe how to organize and use HCP Terraform workspaces and projects

Run triggers connect workspaces so that when a “source” workspace completes a successful apply, HCP Terraform automatically queues a run in the “downstream” workspace. This is commonly used to keep dependent stacks in sync.
feedbacks: Using a run trigger in HCP Terraform allows for the automation of queuing a new run in one workspace after another workspace applies successfully. This helps in orchestrating the workflow and dependencies between different workspaces, ensuring that changes are applied in the correct order.

Providing temporary cloud credentials for authentication purposes is not the purpose of using a run trigger in HCP Terraform. Run triggers are focused on automating the queuing of runs between workspaces, rather than managing authentication credentials.

The purpose of a run trigger is not to force a workspace to always run from the newest commit of its VCS branch. While version control integration is important in Terraform workflows, run triggers specifically focus on the automation of run queuing between workspaces.

Requiring human approval before applying changes in specific workspaces, such as production environments, is not the purpose of using a run trigger in HCP Terraform. Run triggers are designed to automate the workflow and dependencies between workspaces, rather than introducing manual approval steps.

question: You have configured a workspace in HCP Terraform to use local execution. In this mode, what does HCP Terraform do?
questionPlain: You have configured a workspace in HCP Terraform to use local execution. In this mode, what does HCP Terraform do?

choices.text: HCP Terraform only stores and syncs the workspace’s state file, while you run plan and apply locally on your own machine.
HCP Terraform runs all plans and applies in its own environment and streams output back to your CLI session automatically.
Local execution blocks local usage for HCP Terraform and requires every run to start from the UI, with no local CLI interaction allowed.
HCP Terraform replaces the state file with variables and policies so state is no longer required for applies.

explanation:
Objective 8d - Configure and use HCP Terraform integration

Many of HCP Terraform's features rely on remote execution and are not available when using local operations. This includes features like Sentinel policy enforcement, cost estimation, and notifications.

You can disable remote operations for any workspace by changing its Execution Mode to Local. This causes the workspace to act only as a remote backend for Terraform state, with all execution occurring on your own workstations or continuous integration workers.
feedbacks: When using local execution in HCP Terraform, the platform only handles storing and syncing the workspace's state file. This means that you need to run the plan and apply commands locally on your own machine, while HCP Terraform takes care of managing the state file.

This choice is incorrect because in local execution mode, HCP Terraform does not run plans and applies in its own environment. Instead, it delegates these tasks to be performed locally on the user's machine, with the platform focusing on managing the state file.

This choice is incorrect as local execution in HCP Terraform does not block local usage or require every run to start from the UI. Users can still interact with the CLI locally to run plan and apply commands, with the platform handling the state file synchronization.

This choice is incorrect because in local execution mode, HCP Terraform still relies on the state file to track the infrastructure's state. It does not replace the state file with variables and policies, as the state file is essential for managing the infrastructure's lifecycle.

question: Management wants to understand how adopting Infrastructure as Code with Terraform differs from your current method of using the console and CLI to deploy and manage infrastructure. Which statement correctly identifies a major difference?
questionPlain: Management wants to understand how adopting Infrastructure as Code with Terraform differs from your current method of using the console and CLI to deploy and manage infrastructure. Which statement correctly identifies a major difference?

choices.text: Infrastructure as Code allows infrastructure to be described using a configuration syntax that can be versioned, reused, and shared.
Infrastructure as Code requires all resources to be created through APIs instead of UI consoles, while Terraform can work with both approaches.
Infrastructure as Code eliminates the need for cloud provider APIs since all infrastructure is declared in code.
Infrastructure as Code only works with immutable infrastructure patterns, while manual approaches support both mutable and immutable infrastructure.

explanation:
Objective 1a - Explain what IaC is

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) fundamentally transforms infrastructure management by treating infrastructure configuration as code that can be stored in version control systems, reviewed through pull requests, and consistently reproduced across environments. Unlike manual approaches using consoles, CLI tools, or direct API calls, IaC provides a declarative way to define your desired infrastructure state. This enables teams to collaborate more effectively, track infrastructure changes over time, and ensure consistency across deployments through automated provisioning and management.
feedbacks: Infrastructure as Code enables infrastructure to be defined and managed using a configuration syntax, such as Terraform's HCL. This configuration can be stored in version control systems, shared among team members, and reused across different environments. This approach provides consistency, repeatability, and scalability compared to manual deployments through console and CLI.

While Infrastructure as Code promotes creating and managing resources through code, it does not necessarily exclude the use of UI consoles or APIs. Terraform, for example, can interact with cloud provider APIs to provision and manage infrastructure, but the key difference lies in defining infrastructure configurations in code rather than manually through UI consoles.

Infrastructure as Code does not eliminate the need for cloud provider APIs; instead, it leverages these APIs to interact with the underlying infrastructure. By declaring infrastructure configurations in code, teams can automate the provisioning and management of resources, but the APIs are still essential for the actual implementation of the infrastructure changes.

Infrastructure as Code does not dictate specific patterns like immutable or mutable infrastructure. Instead, it provides a way to define and manage infrastructure configurations in a declarative manner. While Infrastructure as Code can support immutable infrastructure patterns, it is not limited to them, and manual approaches can also be used to manage both mutable and immutable infrastructure configurations.

question: What are the advantages of using Infrastructure as Code? (select five)
questionPlain: What are the advantages of using Infrastructure as Code? (select five)

choices.text: Infrastructure as Code enables users to automate a manual task for easier deployment.
Infrastructure as Code is easily repeatable, allowing the user to reuse code to deploy similar yet different resources.
Infrastructure as Code is relatively easy to learn and write, regardless of a user's prior coding experience.
Infrastructure as Code provides configuration consistency and standardization among deployments.
Infrastructure as Code gives the user the ability to recreate an application's infrastructure for disaster recovery scenarios
Infrastructure as Code easily replaces development languages such as Go and .Net for application development

explanation:
Objective 1b - Describe the advantages of IaC patterns

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) refers to the practice of managing and provisioning infrastructure resources through code, rather than manual processes or user interfaces. Some of the benefits of using IaC include:

  1. Consistency and repeatability: IaC allows for the creation of infrastructure in a consistent and repeatable way. This ensures that the same infrastructure can be deployed across multiple environments (e.g. development, testing, production) with minimal differences, reducing the risk of issues due to configuration drift or environment-specific issues.

  2. Speed and agility: IaC enables the rapid provisioning and scaling of infrastructure resources, thereby reducing the time required to set up and modify infrastructure. This enables teams to quickly respond to changing business needs or shifting workloads, without the delays associated with manual provisioning processes.

  3. Version control: IaC code can be stored in version control systems, allowing teams to track changes over time and revert to previous versions if necessary. This provides a history of infrastructure changes, ensuring that teams always work with the most up-to-date version of the infrastructure code.

  4. Collaboration and documentation: IaC code can be shared and collaborated on, allowing teams to work together to design and maintain infrastructure resources. It also provides a single source of truth for documentation, making it easier to understand how the infrastructure is configured and how it has changed over time.

  5. Cost savings: IaC can help reduce infrastructure costs by enabling teams to manage resources more effectively, optimize usage, and avoid over-provisioning. It can also reduce the need for manual intervention, saving time and minimizing the risk of errors.

Overall, using IaC can help organizations achieve greater consistency, speed, agility, collaboration, and cost savings in their infrastructure management practices.
feedbacks: Infrastructure as Code allows users to automate the manual task of provisioning and managing infrastructure, making deployment easier, faster, and more efficient.
By using Infrastructure as Code, users can easily repeat the deployment process by reusing code, which is particularly useful for deploying similar resources with slight variations.
Infrastructure as Code is designed to be user-friendly and relatively simple to learn and write, making it accessible to users with varying levels of coding experience.
Infrastructure as Code ensures configuration consistency and standardization across deployments, reducing the risk of errors and ensuring that all environments are set up identically.
With Infrastructure as Code, users can quickly and accurately rebuild an application's infrastructure in disaster recovery scenarios, ensuring business continuity and minimizing downtime.

Infrastructure as Code is not intended to replace development languages like Go and .Net for application development. Instead, it focuses on automating infrastructure provisioning and management tasks.

question: What benefits would you see by using a multi-cloud and provider-agnostic tool like Terraform? (select two)
questionPlain: What benefits would you see by using a multi-cloud and provider-agnostic tool like Terraform? (select two)

choices.text: Reduces operational overhead by allowing teams to learn and govern a single tool across all environments.
Delivers a consistent declarative workflow and language across providers and hypervisors.
Removes the need for provider-specific credentials or authentication flows.
Programmatically standardizes pricing and usage models across all cloud platforms.

explanation:
Objective 1c - Explain how Terraform manages multi-cloud, hybrid cloud, and service-agnostic workflows

A common workflow (initiate/plan/apply) enhances consistency, and using a single tool lowers training, governance, and CI/CD complexity. The other statements overpromise because providers still vary, credentials are still needed, and pricing/behavior are not automatically standardized.
feedbacks: Using a multi-cloud and provider-agnostic tool like Terraform reduces operational overhead by enabling teams to manage infrastructure across different cloud providers using a single tool. This streamlines the learning process and governance, as teams only need to become proficient in one tool for all environments.

Terraform provides a consistent declarative workflow and language across various cloud providers and hypervisors. This consistency allows for easier management of infrastructure and deployments, as the same syntax and workflow can be used regardless of the underlying provider.

While Terraform helps manage infrastructure across multiple cloud providers, it still requires provider-specific credentials and authentication flows to interact with each cloud platform. Terraform abstracts away the complexity of managing infrastructure, but it does not eliminate the need for provider-specific authentication.

Terraform does not programmatically standardize pricing and usage models across all cloud platforms. Pricing and usage models are specific to each cloud provider and are not standardized by Terraform. Terraform focuses on infrastructure as code and automation, rather than pricing and billing aspects of cloud services.

question: Before a new Terraform provider can be used in a configuration, what steps are required? (select two)
questionPlain: Before a new Terraform provider can be used in a configuration, what steps are required? (select two)

choices.text: Declare and configure the provider in the configuration with the required arguments.
Initialize the working directory using terraform init to download and install the provider.
Add the provider name and configuration to terraform.tfvars and pass it with -var at runtime.
Run terraform validate to compile the configuration and fetch the plugin from the Terraform registry.

explanation:
Objective 2a - Install and version Terraform providers

Each time a new provider is added to the configuration, either explicitly via a provider block or by adding a resource from that provider, Terraform must initialize the provider before it can be used. Initialization downloads and installs the provider's plugin, allowing it to be executed later.
feedbacks: Declaring and configuring the provider in the Terraform configuration file is essential to inform Terraform about the new provider and provide any necessary configuration arguments. This step allows Terraform to understand how to interact with the new provider during the infrastructure provisioning process.

Initializing the working directory using terraform init is crucial to download and install the required provider plugin. This step ensures that Terraform has access to the necessary plugin to communicate with the new provider and execute the configuration successfully.

Adding the provider name and configuration to terraform.tfvars and passing it with -var at runtime is not a required step for enabling a new Terraform provider in a configuration. terraform.tfvars is typically used for variable definitions, and passing provider configuration in this manner may not be the most appropriate approach.

Running terraform validate It is used to check the syntax and configuration of the Terraform files, but does not directly relate to enabling a new provider in the configuration. This command does not fetch plugins from the Terraform registry; instead, it validates the configuration for any errors or issues.

question: In the top-level terraform block, which setting specifies a provider’s source and version constraints?
questionPlain: In the top-level terraform block, which setting specifies a provider’s source and version constraints?

choices.text: required_providers
provider
required_version
backend

explanation:
Objective 2a - Install and version Terraform providers

To identify a specific version of a provider in Terraform, you can use the required_providers configuration block. This block enables you to specify the provider's name and the version range you want to use by utilizing Terraform's version constraint syntax.

Here's an example of how to use the required_providers block to specify a specific version of the AWS provider:


terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "6.5.0"
    }
  }
}

In this example, we're specifying that we require version 6.5.0 of the AWS provider, which is hosted at the hashicorp/aws source. Note that the version constraint syntax allows you to specify a range of versions using operators such as >= and <=.

When you run terraform init with this configuration, Terraform will download and install the specified version of the AWS provider, and will use it for all subsequent Terraform commands for that module. If the specified version is not available, Terraform will return an error and fail to initialize the configuration.
feedbacks: The required_providers setting in the top-level terraform block is used to specify a provider's source and version constraints. This setting allows you to define which providers are required for your Terraform configuration and the specific versions that should be used.

The provider setting in the top-level terraform block is used to configure a specific provider for a particular resource or module within your Terraform configuration. It is not used to specify a provider's source and version constraints at the top level.

The required_version setting in the top-level terraform block is used to specify the minimum version of Terraform required to run the configuration. It is not used to define a provider's source and version constraints.
The backend setting in the top-level terraform block is used to configure the backend where Terraform stores its state data. It is not used to specify a provider's source and version constraints.

question: Why should a user specify provider version constraints in their Terraform configuration?
questionPlain: Why should a user specify provider version constraints in their Terraform configuration?

choices.text: providers are released on a separate schedule from Terraform itself; therefore, a newer version could introduce breaking changes
to ensure that the provider version matches the version of Terraform you are using
to remove older versions of the provider
to match the version number of your application being deployed via Terraform

explanation:
Objective 2a - Install and version Terraform providers

Declaring the required version of a provider in a Terraform configuration file is a good idea for several reasons:


  1. Reproducibility: By specifying the exact version of a provider, you can ensure that anyone running your Terraform configuration uses the same version of the provider as you. This makes your infrastructure configuration more reproducible and helps avoid issues that can arise when different versions of a provider are used.

  2. Predictability: When you specify a specific provider version, you can be confident that your infrastructure configuration will behave predictably, regardless of changes to the provider in future versions. This can help you avoid surprises and reduce the risk of unintended consequences.

  3. Compatibility: Different versions of a provider may have varying APIs, resources, or behaviors, which can cause issues if you switch to a new version without being aware of the differences. By specifying the required version of a provider in your Terraform configuration, you can ensure that your configuration remains compatible with the specific version of the provider you have tested and validated.

  4. Version locking: When you specify the required version of a provider in your Terraform configuration, you effectively lock the provider's version to that version, unless you explicitly change it. This can help prevent issues that may arise when using a different, potentially incompatible version of the provider.

In summary, specifying the required version of a provider in your Terraform configuration file helps ensure that your infrastructure configuration is more predictable, reproducible, and compatible, and reduces the risk of unintended consequences or issues caused by version differences.
feedbacks: Providers are developed and released independently of Terraform, so newer versions may introduce breaking changes that could impact the functionality of your infrastructure. Specifying version constraints ensures that you are using a compatible provider version with your Terraform configuration.

While it is important to ensure that the provider version matches the version of Terraform you are using, the primary reason for specifying provider version constraints is to prevent potential breaking changes that could occur with newer versions of the provider.

Specifying provider version constraints does not necessarily remove older versions of the provider. It simply ensures that your Terraform configuration uses a specific version or range of versions to maintain consistency and stability in your infrastructure.

Matching the provider version with the version number of your application being deployed is not the main reason for specifying provider version constraints. The primary purpose is to prevent compatibility issues and breaking changes that could arise from using an incompatible provider version with your Terraform configuration.

question: Which of the following is considered a Terraform plugin?
questionPlain: Which of the following is considered a Terraform plugin?

choices.text: provider
module
backend
variable

explanation:
Objective 2b - Describe how Terraform uses providers

In Terraform, a plugin is a binary executable that implements a specific provider. A provider is a plugin that allows Terraform to manage a specific cloud provider or service.

When Terraform runs, it loads the plugins required to manage the resources specified in the configuration files. Each provider has its own plugin, and Terraform loads the plugins for the providers specified in the configuration.

The plugin is responsible for interacting with the cloud provider's API, translating Terraform configurations into API calls, and managing the state of the resources that Terraform manages.

Plugins are stored in the Terraform plugin cache, a directory on the local machine that contains the binary executables for each plugin. When Terraform runs, it looks for plugins in the cache and automatically downloads any missing plugins from the Terraform Registry or a specified source.

Terraform plugins are written in Go and follow a specific plugin protocol, which defines the interactions between Terraform and the plugin. The plugin protocol allows Terraform to communicate with the plugin and provides a standard way for plugins to manage resources across different providers.

https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin
feedbacks: A Terraform provider is a plugin that interacts with a specific type of infrastructure, such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. Providers are responsible for understanding API interactions and exposing resources for Terraform to manage, making them an essential component of Terraform configurations.

A Terraform module is a reusable collection of resources that can be used across different Terraform configurations. While modules are a fundamental concept in Terraform for organizing and reusing code, they are not considered plugins like providers.

A Terraform backend is a configuration setting that determines where state data is stored and how Terraform operations are executed. Backends define how Terraform interacts with remote storage services like AWS S3 or HashiCorp Consul, but they are not considered plugins in the same way that providers are.

A Terraform variable is a parameter that can be passed into Terraform configurations to make them more flexible and reusable. Variables allow users to customize configurations without modifying the underlying code, but they are not classified as plugins like providers.

question: Which of the following best describes a Terraform provider?
questionPlain: Which of the following best describes a Terraform provider?

choices.text: a plugin that Terraform uses to translate the API interactions with the service or provider
describes an infrastructure object, such as a virtual network, compute instance, or other components
serves as a parameter for a Terraform module that allows a module to be customized
a container for multiple resources that are used together

explanation:
Objective 2b - Describe how Terraform uses providers

In Terraform, a provider is a plugin that enables Terraform to interact with a specific cloud or service provider, such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform (GCP). Providers are responsible for understanding the APIs and resources the target infrastructure platform provides and for translating Terraform configuration code into API calls that can create, read, update, and delete resources.

Each provider typically consists of resource types, data sources, and other settings that define the provider's capabilities within Terraform. These resources and data sources correspond to the resources that can be managed within the target infrastructure, such as virtual machines, storage accounts, or network interfaces.

To use a provider in Terraform, you must first configure it in your Terraform code by specifying the provider's name and any required configuration settings, such as access keys, secret keys, or region. Once the provider is configured, you can then use its resources and data sources in your Terraform code to define the infrastructure you want to manage.

Terraform has a large and growing ecosystem of third-party providers that support a wide range of infrastructure platforms and services, as well as an official set of core providers maintained by HashiCorp, the company behind Terraform. The availability and quality of providers is a crucial factor in the usefulness of Terraform as a tool for managing infrastructure as code.
feedbacks: A Terraform provider is a plugin that Terraform uses to interact with a specific service or provider. It translates the API interactions between Terraform and the service, allowing Terraform to manage resources in that service.

This choice describes a Terraform resource, not a provider. A Terraform resource represents an infrastructure object like a virtual network or compute instance that Terraform manages within a provider.
This choice describes a Terraform module parameter, not a provider. Module parameters allow customization of a module's behavior and configuration, but they are not directly related to providers.

This choice does not accurately describe a Terraform provider. While a provider can manage multiple resources, it is not a container for resources but rather a plugin that facilitates interactions with a specific service or provider.

question: True or False? Multiple providers can be declared within a single Terraform configuration file.
questionPlain: True or False? Multiple providers can be declared within a single Terraform configuration file.

choices.text: True
False

explanation:
Objective 2c - Write Terraform configuration using multiple providers

Multiple providers can be declared within a single Terraform configuration file. In fact, it is common to declare multiple providers within a single configuration file, particularly when managing resources across multiple cloud providers.

When declaring multiple providers within a single configuration file, each provider should have a unique configuration block that specifies its name, source, and any required settings or credentials. Here's an example of what a configuration block for two different providers might look like:


terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "6.5.0"
    }
    google = {
      source = "hashicorp/google"
      version = "4.5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-west-2"
}

provider "google" {
  project = "my-project"
}


In this example, we have declared two providers (aws and google) within a single configuration file. The terraform block declares the required providers, while the provider blocks specify the provider-specific settings and credentials.
feedbacks: True. Multiple providers can indeed be declared within a single Terraform configuration file. This allows users to manage resources from different cloud providers or services within the same Terraform configuration, making it easier to orchestrate complex infrastructure setups.

This statement is incorrect as Terraform allows users to declare and configure multiple providers within a single configuration file. This flexibility enables users to manage resources across different cloud platforms or services seamlessly within the same Terraform setup.

question: Which statements are true about provider configurations in modules? (select three)
questionPlain: Which statements are true about provider configurations in modules? (select three)

choices.text: Child modules automatically inherit the default provider configurations from their parent module
Modules containing provider blocks cannot be used with the for_each argument
The providers argument in a module block allows explicit passing of specific provider configurations
Child modules must always define their own provider blocks for proper isolation
Modules with provider blocks can still be used with depends_on if providers are passed explicitly

explanation:
Objective 2c - Write Terraform configuration using multiple providers

Providers can be passed to child modules either implicitly (automatic inheritance of default providers) or explicitly (using the providers argument). Modules intended to be called by other modules must not contain provider blocks, as this makes them incompatible with for_each, count, and depends_on arguments. Child modules should receive their provider configurations from the calling module rather than defining their own.
feedbacks: Child modules automatically inherit the default provider configurations from their parent module. This allows for a seamless propagation of provider configurations throughout the module hierarchy without the need for explicit redefinition in each child module.

A module intended to be called by one or more other modules must not contain any provider blocks. A module containing its own provider configurations is not compatible with the for_each, count, and depends_on arguments.

The providers argument in a module block allows explicit passing of specific provider configurations. This feature enables users to define and pass specific provider configurations to a module, providing flexibility and customization in managing provider settings within the module.

Child modules do not always have to define their own provider blocks for proper isolation. Inheritance of provider configurations from parent modules can provide the necessary isolation and consistency in provider settings across the module hierarchy without the need for redundant definitions in each child module.

A module intended to be called by one or more other modules must not contain any provider blocks. A module containing its own provider configurations is not compatible with the for_each, count, and depends_on arguments.

question: You run terraform plan in a workspace that has existing infrastructure. Terraform shows that it will update 3 resources, create 2 new resources, and destroy 1 resource. How does Terraform determine what changes need to be made?
questionPlain: You run terraform plan in a workspace that has existing infrastructure. Terraform shows that it will update 3 resources, create 2 new resources, and destroy 1 resource. How does Terraform determine what changes need to be made?

choices.text: Terraform compares the desired state in the configuration with the current state in the state file to build the plan
Terraform queries the cloud provider APIs to discover all resources and compares them to the configuration file
Terraform reads the previous plan output file and applies any changes that weren't completed
Terraform uses specific cloud provider services to identify resources that have drifted

explanation:
Objective 2d - Explain how Terraform uses and manages state

When you run terraform plan, Terraform combines your configuration with the stored state, refreshing that state from the real infrastructure as necessary. It then compares “what exists now” (state plus refresh) with “what you want” (configuration) to calculate a set of proposed actions. This comparison is only possible because Terraform maintains a state record of remote objects and their attributes between runs.
feedbacks: Terraform determines changes by comparing the desired state defined in the configuration files with the current state stored in the state file. This process allows Terraform to identify what resources need to be updated, created, or destroyed based on the configuration changes.
Terraform does not scan or discover all resources in the provider account. It refreshes only the resources already in the state file and compares that refreshed state to the configuration.

Terraform does not read the previous plan output file to determine changes when running a new plan. Each new plan execution compares the configuration's desired state with the current state in the state file to generate an updated plan.

Terraform does not rely on specific cloud provider services to identify resource drift when running a plan. The comparison is made between the configuration files and the state file to determine the necessary changes in the infrastructure.

question: What are the three core steps that make up the Terraform workflow? (select three)
questionPlain: What are the three core steps that make up the Terraform workflow? (select three)

choices.text: Write - Author infrastructure as code.
Plan - Preview changes before applying.
Apply - Provision reproducible infrastructure.
Validate - Verify the syntax and internal consistency
Destroy - Deprovision and remove all infrastructure resources
Import - Bring in existing infrastructure resources under management

explanation:
Objective 3a - Describe the Terraform workflow

The core Terraform workflow has three steps:

  1. Write - Author infrastructure as code.

  2. Plan - Preview changes before applying.

  3. Apply - Provision reproducible infrastructure.
feedbacks: Writing infrastructure as code is a core step in the Terraform workflow as it allows users to define and manage their infrastructure in a declarative manner.
Planning is an essential step in the Terraform workflow as it allows users to preview the changes that will be applied to the infrastructure before actually making those changes.
Applying the changes is a crucial step in the Terraform workflow as it provisions the defined infrastructure in a reproducible manner based on the code written and the plan generated.
Validating the syntax and internal consistency is not one of the core steps in the Terraform workflow. While validation is important, it is typically done during the writing and planning stages.

Destroying infrastructure resources is an important step in the Terraform workflow, but it is not one of the core steps. Destruction typically occurs after applying changes and when infrastructure needs to be deprovisioned.

Importing existing infrastructure resources under management is not one of the core steps in the Terraform workflow. Importing is a useful feature for managing existing resources, but it is not part of the fundamental workflow steps.

question: Which of the following actions are performed during a terraform init? (select three)
questionPlain: Which of the following actions are performed during a terraform init? (select three)

choices.text: downloads the required modules referenced in the configuration
downloads the providers/plugins required to execute the configuration
initializes the backend configuration
provisions the declared resources in your configuration

explanation:
Objective 3b - Initialize a Terraform working directory

The terraform init command is used to initialize a working directory containing Terraform configuration files. This is the first command that should be run after writing a new Terraform configuration or cloning an existing one from version control. It is safe to run this command multiple times.
feedbacks: During a terraform init, Terraform downloads the required modules referenced in the configuration. This ensures that all necessary modules are available locally for use in the Terraform configuration.

terraform init also downloads the providers/plugins required to execute the configuration. Providers are responsible for understanding API interactions and exposing resources for Terraform to manage, ensuring that Terraform can interact with the specified cloud or infrastructure services by downloading them.

Another action performed during a terraform init is initializing the backend configuration. The backend configuration specifies where state data is stored and how operations should be performed, so initializing it is crucial for managing the infrastructure's state.

Provisioning the declared resources in your configuration is not an action performed during a terraform init. Provisioning resources typically occurs after running terraform apply, where Terraform creates, updates, or deletes resources based on the configuration provided.

question: What is the .terraform.lock.hcl file and when does Terraform create or modify it?
questionPlain: What is the .terraform.lock.hcl file and when does Terraform create or modify it?

choices.text: The .terraform.lock.hcl file is a dependency lock file used by Terraform. It is created or updated every time you run terraform init.
The .terraform.lock.hcl file is a state snapshot used by Terraform. It is created or updated every time you run terraform apply.
The .terraform.lock.hcl file contains backend connection and credentials settings. It is created or updated every time you modify the backend.
The .terraform.lock.hcl file is a concurrency lock to prevent simultaneous runs. It is created or updated every time you run a terraform plan.

explanation:
Objective 3b - Initialize a Terraform working directory

The dependency lock file is a file that belongs to the configuration as a whole, rather than to each separate module in the configuration. For that reason, Terraform creates it and expects to find it in your current working directory when you run Terraform, which is also the directory containing the .tf files for the root module of your configuration.

The lock file is always named .terraform.lock.hcl, and this name is intended to signify that it is a lock file for various items that Terraform caches in the .terraform subdirectory of your working directory.

Terraform automatically creates or updates the dependency lock file each time you run the terraform init command. You should include this file in your version control repository so that you can discuss potential changes to your external dependencies via code review, just as you would discuss potential changes to your configuration itself.
feedbacks: The .terraform.lock.hcl file is a dependency lock file that Terraform uses to ensure consistent dependency versions across different runs. It is created or updated every time you run terraform init to initialize the working directory and download the necessary providers and modules.

The .terraform.lock.hcl file is not a state snapshot but a dependency lock file. It is not created or updated during terraform apply, which is used to apply changes to infrastructure based on the Terraform configuration.

The .terraform.lock.hcl file does not contain backend connection and credentials settings. It is specifically used for managing dependencies and versions in Terraform. It is not created or updated when modifying the backend configuration.

The .terraform.lock.hcl file is not a concurrency lock but a dependency lock file. It is not created or updated during a terraform plan, which is used to generate an execution plan for changes to infrastructure.

question: Bryan is drafting new Terraform code and wants to verify that the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent without contacting any remote services. Which command should he run?
questionPlain: Bryan is drafting new Terraform code and wants to verify that the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent without contacting any remote services. Which command should he run?

choices.text: terraform validate
terraform fmt
terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform show

explanation:
Objective 3c - Validate a Terraform configuration

The terraform validate command validates the configuration files in a directory, referring only to the configuration and not accessing any remote services such as remote state, provider APIs, etc.

Validate runs checks that verify whether a configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent, regardless of any provided variables or existing state. It is thus primarily useful for general verification of reusable modules, including correctness of attribute names and value types.
feedbacks: The terraform validate command is used to check whether the configuration files are syntactically valid and internally consistent without accessing any remote services. It is a quick way to ensure that the code is correctly written and structured before applying it.

The terraform fmt command is used to automatically format Terraform configuration files to a consistent style. While it helps maintain code readability and consistency, it does not specifically validate the syntax or internal consistency of the code like the terraform validate command does.

The terraform apply -refresh-only command is used to apply changes to the infrastructure while only refreshing the state without making any actual changes. It does not perform a validation check on the code to ensure its syntactic validity and internal consistency.

The terraform show command is used to display the current state or configuration of Terraform-managed infrastructure. It does not perform a validation check on the code to ensure its syntactic validity and internal consistency like the terraform validate command does.

question: You're refactoring a large Terraform configuration, splitting a monolithic file into multiple smaller files and reorganizing resource blocks. Before running terraform plan, what's the fastest way to verify you didn't introduce any syntax errors during the refactoring?
questionPlain: You're refactoring a large Terraform configuration, splitting a monolithic file into multiple smaller files and reorganizing resource blocks. Before running terraform plan, what's the fastest way to verify you didn't introduce any syntax errors during the refactoring?

choices.text: run terraform validate
run terraform init
run terraform plan
run terraform fmt -recursive

explanation:
Objective 3c - Validate a Terraform configuration

After refactoring configuration files, terraform validate is the fastest way to catch syntax errors, typos, and internal consistency issues without having to wait for a full plan operation. Unlike terraform plan, validate doesn't communicate with your cloud provider or check state, making it much faster for quick syntax verification.
feedbacks: Running terraform validate is the fastest way to verify that you didn't introduce any syntax errors during the refactoring process. This command checks the configuration files for syntax errors, ensuring your Terraform code is valid and can be executed successfully.

Running terraform init initializes the Terraform working directory and downloads any necessary plugins. While this step is important before applying changes, it does not specifically verify syntax errors in the configuration files.

Running terraform plan generates an execution plan for Terraform, showing what actions will be taken when the configuration is applied. While this step is crucial before making changes, it does not specifically check for syntax errors introduced during refactoring.

Running terraform fmt -recursive formats the Terraform configuration files according to the Terraform style conventions. While this can help maintain consistency in the codebase, it does not directly verify syntax errors that may have been introduced during the refactoring process.

question: After executing a terraform plan in your working directory, you notice that a resource has a tilde (~) next to it. What does this indicate?
questionPlain: After executing a terraform plan in your working directory, you notice that a resource has a tilde (~) next to it. What does this indicate?

choices.text: the resource will be destroyed and recreated
the resource will be updated in place
the resource will be created
Terraform can't determine how to proceed due to a problem with the state file

explanation:
Objective 3d - Generate and review an execution plan for Terraform

The prefix -/+ means that Terraform will destroy and recreate the resource, rather than updating it in-place. Some attributes and resources can be updated in-place and are shown with the ~ prefix.
feedbacks: Incorrect. The tilde (~) next to a resource in the terraform plan output indicates that the resource will be updated in place, meaning Terraform will make changes to the existing resource without destroying and recreating it.

When a resource has a tilde (~) next to it in the terraform plan, it signifies that the resource will be updated in place, preserving its current state and making necessary modifications without recreating it.

The presence of a tilde (~) next to a resource in the terraform plan does not indicate that the resource will be created. Instead, it suggests that the resource will be updated in place, maintaining its existing state.

If a resource has a tilde (~) next to it in the terraform plan, it does not mean that Terraform can't determine how to proceed due to a problem with the state file. Instead, it signifies that the resource will be updated in place, without being destroyed and recreated.

question: You’ve updated a module and run terraform plan with default settings against the workspace’s remote state. What happens when the command is executed?
questionPlain: You’ve updated a module and run terraform plan with default settings against the workspace’s remote state. What happens when the command is executed?

choices.text: Terraform creates an execution plan and determines what changes are required to achieve the desired state in the configuration files.
Terraform applies the changes required in the target infrastructure in order to reach the desired configuration
Terraform initializes the backend and the working directory is prepped
Terraform reconciles the state it knows about with the real-world infrastructure

explanation:
Objective 3d - Generate and review an execution plan for Terraform

The terraform plan command is used to create an execution plan. Terraform performs a refresh, unless explicitly disabled, and then determines what actions are necessary to achieve the desired state specified in the configuration files.

After a plan has been run, it can be executed by running a terraform apply

https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan
feedbacks: When a terraform plan is executed, it creates an execution plan by analyzing the current state of the infrastructure and the desired state specified in the configuration files. It determines what changes need to be made to achieve the desired configuration without actually applying those changes.

Applying changes to the target infrastructure to reach the desired configuration is the role of the terraform apply command, not terraform plan. Terraform plan is used to preview the changes that will be made before actually applying them.

Initializing the backend and preparing the working directory are tasks performed by the terraform init command, not terraform plan. Terraform plan focuses on generating an execution plan based on the configuration files.

terraform plan does refresh existing resources as part of building the plan, but this answer is incomplete because it doesn’t mention creating the execution plan and implies that reconciling state is the only behavior.

question: What happens when a terraform apply command is executed?
questionPlain: What happens when a terraform apply command is executed?

choices.text: the backend is initialized and the working directory is prepped
creates the execution plan for the deployment of resources
applies the changes required in the target infrastructure in order to reach the desired configuration
reconciles the state Terraform knows about with the real-world infrastructure

explanation:
Objective 3e - Apply changes to infrastructure with Terraform

The terraform apply command is used to apply the changes required to reach the desired state of the configuration, or the pre-determined set of actions generated by a terraform plan execution plan.
feedbacks: Initializing the backend and preparing the working directory are tasks that are typically performed before executing the terraform apply command. These steps ensure that Terraform has the necessary configuration and access to the backend to apply changes to the infrastructure.

Creating the execution plan is a step that precedes the terraform apply command. The execution plan outlines the actions that Terraform will take to achieve the desired configuration; however, it does not represent the actual application of changes to the infrastructure.

The terraform apply command is responsible for applying the changes specified in the Terraform configuration to the target infrastructure. It ensures that the infrastructure matches the desired state defined in the configuration files.

Reconciling the state is a process that occurs during the terraform apply command. It compares the current state of the infrastructure with the state that Terraform knows about and makes any necessary changes to align the infrastructure with the desired configuration.

question:

question: Which Terraform command will force a resource to be destroyed and recreated even if there are no configuration changes that would require it?
questionPlain: Which Terraform command will force a resource to be destroyed and recreated even if there are no configuration changes that would require it?

choices.text: terraform apply -replace=<address>
terraform fmt
terraform apply -refresh-only
terraform destroy

explanation:
Objective 3f - Destroy Terraform-managed infrastructure

The terraform apply -replace=<address> command manually marks a Terraform-managed resource to be replaced, forcing it to be destroyed and recreated during the apply. Even if there are no configuration changes that would require a change or deletion of this resource, this command will instruct Terraform to replace it. This can come in handy if a resource has become degraded or damaged outside of Terraform.

https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/apply#replace-resource
feedbacks: The terraform apply -replace= command is used to force a resource to be destroyed and recreated, even if there are no configuration changes that would require it. This is achieved by specifying the resource address that needs to be replaced, ensuring that the resource is recreated with the latest configuration.

The terraform fmt command is used to format Terraform configuration files to ensure consistency and readability. It does not force a resource to be destroyed and recreated, regardless of configuration changes.

The terraform apply -refresh-only command is used to update the state file with the latest real-world infrastructure information without making any changes to the resources. It does not force a resource to be destroyed and recreated, even if there are no configuration changes that would require it.

The terraform destroy command is used to destroy all resources defined in the Terraform configuration. It does not force a specific resource to be destroyed and recreated, regardless of configuration changes.

question: Your team wants to enforce consistent formatting across all Terraform files before merging code into the main branch. You're setting up a CI/CD pipeline and need a command that checks whether files are properly formatted without making changes. Which command should you use?
questionPlain: Your team wants to enforce consistent formatting across all Terraform files before merging code into the main branch. You're setting up a CI/CD pipeline and need a command that checks whether files are properly formatted without making changes. Which command should you use?

choices.text: terraform fmt -check
terraform fmt -diff

explanation:
Objective 3g - Apply formatting and style adjustments to a configuration
