It checks whether files are properly formatted according to Terraform style conventions without changing the files. If formatting issues are found, the command exits with a non-zero status code, which can cause the pipeline to fail and alert developers to run terraform fmt before committing. This is the standard approach for enforcing code formatting standards in automated workflows.
feedbacks: The terraform fmt -check command is used to check whether Terraform files are properly formatted without making any changes. It validates file formatting and ensures consistency across all files in the repository before merging into the main branch.

The terraform fmt -diff command is used to show the differences between the current formatting of Terraform files and the formatted version. It does not check whether files are properly formatted without making changes, so it is not the correct command for enforcing consistent formatting.
The terraform fmt -validate command does not exist in Terraform commands. It is not a valid command for checking Terraform file formatting without making changes.

The terraform validate -format command is not the correct command for checking the formatting of Terraform files. The terraform validate command is used to validate the configuration files for syntax errors, while the -format flag is not a valid option for the validate command.

question: Your company has a centralized network team that manages all Azure Virtual Networks. Your application team needs to deploy virtual machines into the prod-network VNet, which the network team created. What is the correct approach in your Terraform configuration?
questionPlain: Your company has a centralized network team that manages all Azure Virtual Networks. Your application team needs to deploy virtual machines into the prod-network VNet, which the network team created. What is the correct approach in your Terraform configuration?

choices.text: use a data block to reference the existing VNet, then create your VM resources that use attributes from the data source
use a resource block to import the existing VNet into your state, then create your VM resources
create a new resource block for the VNet with the same name, then create your VM resources
contact the network team to add a depends_on relationship between their VNet and your VMs

explanation:
Objective 4a - Use and differentiate resource and data blocks

When infrastructure is managed by another team or process, use a data block to query and reference the existing resource rather than trying to manage it yourself. The data block lets you retrieve attributes of the existing VNet (such as its ID, address space, etc.) that you need for your VM configuration, without taking ownership of the VNet in your state file. This maintains clear ownership boundaries. The network team continues to manage the VNet through their own Terraform configuration, while your team can reference it safely without conflicts.
feedbacks: Using a data block to reference the existing VNet allows you to retrieve information about the prod-network VNet created by the network team without modifying it. This approach ensures that your VM resources can be created with the correct attributes from the existing VNet.

Importing the existing VNet into your state using a resource block may cause conflicts or inconsistencies with the centrally managed VNet by the network team. It is not recommended to import existing infrastructure into your Terraform state without proper coordination with the network team.

Creating a new resource block for the VNet with the same name as the centrally managed VNet may lead to naming conflicts and inconsistencies in the network configuration. It is important to avoid creating duplicate resources, especially when working with centrally managed infrastructure.

Contacting the network team to add a depends_on relationship between their VNet and your VMs is not the correct approach in Terraform configuration. Terraform manages dependencies automatically based on resource relationships defined in the configuration. It is not necessary to manually add dependencies between resources managed by different teams.

question:
A module creates VMs with the vSphere provider. It includes arguments such as datastore = "DS1", network_label = "VM Network", and a folder = "Dev/Apps". You need the same module to work in Lab, QA, and Prod vCenter environments without code changes.

What is the most appropriate change to enable the reuse of this module?
questionPlain: A module creates VMs with the vSphere provider. It includes arguments such as datastore = "DS1", network_label = "VM Network", and a folder = "Dev/Apps". You need the same module to work in Lab, QA, and Prod vCenter environments without code changes.What is the most appropriate change to enable the reuse of this module?

choices.text: Convert the hard-coded values to input variables and provide environment-specific settings via tfvars or variable sets at plan/apply.
Put the values in locals and commit separate branches per environment so the module references different locals.
Add preconditions that fail when the environment differs, forcing operators to update the file when switching sites.
Create outputs for these values and reference them from a second “override” module that runs after the first.

explanation:
Objective 4c - Use variables and outputs

Input variables serve as parameters for a Terraform module, allowing aspects of the module to be customized without altering the module's source code, and enabling modules to be shared across different configurations.
feedbacks: By converting the hard-coded values to input variables, you can provide environment-specific settings via tfvars or variable sets at plan/apply. This approach enables easy customization of the module for Lab, QA, and Production vCenter environments without requiring modifications to the core module code.

Putting the values in locals and committing separate branches per environment may lead to code duplication and maintenance overhead. It is not the most efficient way to handle environment-specific settings and may result in confusion and complexity when managing multiple branches.

Adding preconditions that fail when the environment differs and forcing operators to update the file when switching sites is not a scalable or practical solution. It introduces unnecessary manual steps and potential errors when switching between environments, making it less suitable for enabling reuse of the module.

Creating outputs for these values and referencing them from a second "override" module that runs after the first can add unnecessary complexity to the module structure. It introduces an additional layer of abstraction and may make the code harder to maintain and understand, especially when dealing with multiple environments.

question: Which of the following options correctly demonstrates the HCL syntax for assigning a value to a variable declared with the type map(string)?
questionPlain: Which of the following options correctly demonstrates the HCL syntax for assigning a value to a variable declared with the type map(string)?

question:
In an expression, how do you correctly reference the build-tag value from the variable declaration below?

lookup(var.metadata, build-tag, "")
var["metadata"]["build-tag"]

To read a value from a map, use bracket (index) syntax with the key as a string: var.metadata["build-tag"]. Dot syntax like var.metadata.build-tag does not work here because build-tag contains a hyphen, and Terraform would try to interpret it as the expression build minus tag. Bracket syntax also handles keys with spaces, dots, or other characters that are not valid identifiers.
feedbacks: To correctly reference the build-tag value in the variable declaration, you should use the syntax var.metadata["build-tag"]. This syntax allows you to access the value associated with the key build-tag in the map variable metadata.

Using var.metadata.build-tag to reference the build-tag value is incorrect in this context. When accessing a value with a key in a map, you should use the syntax var.metadata["key"] to ensure proper referencing.

The lookup function in Terraform is used to retrieve a value from a map variable based on a specified key. However, in this case, the correct way to reference the build-tag value is var.metadata["build-tag"], not lookup(var.metadata, build-tag, "").

The syntax var["metadata"]["build-tag"] is not the correct way to reference the build-tag value in the variable declaration. To access the value associated with the key build-tag in the map variable metadata, you should use var.metadata["build-tag"].

question: Your team maintains a map of common tags to apply to all resources. Each individual resource also needs its own specific tags. questionPlain: Your team maintains a map of common tags to apply to all resources. Each individual resource also needs its own specific tags. To accomplish this, you have var.common_tags containing shared tags and local.resource_tags containing resource-specific tags. How do you combine both to apply to a resource?

concat(var.common_tags, local.resource_tags)
join(var.common_tags, local.resource_tags)
flatten(var.common_tags, local.resource_tags)

explanation:
Objective 4e - Write dynamic configuration using expressions and functions

The merge() function takes two or more maps and combines them into a single map. When there are duplicate keys, values from maps later in the argument list take precedence. This makes it perfect for combining common tags with resource-specific tags, with the latter overriding the former if needed.
feedbacks: The merge() function is used to combine two maps into a single map in Terraform. In this scenario, var.common_tags and local.resource_tags are maps containing tags, so using merge(var.common_tags, local.resource_tags) will combine the shared tags with the resource-specific tags to apply them to the resource effectively.

The concat() function is used to concatenate lists or tuples in Terraform, not maps. Since var.common_tags and local.resource_tags are maps in this case, using concat(var.common_tags, local.resource_tags) would not be the correct way to combine them for applying tags to a resource. The merge() function is used to combine two maps into a single map in Terraform.

The join() function is used to concatenate elements of a list into a single string with a specified delimiter. It is not suitable for combining maps like var.common_tags and local.resource_tags to apply tags to a resource. The merge() function is used to combine two maps into a single map in Terraform.

The flatten() function is used to flatten a list of lists into a single list in Terraform. It is not designed to combine maps like var.common_tags and local.resource_tags, so using flatten(var.common_tags, local.resource_tags) would not achieve the desired result of applying both shared and resource-specific tags to a resource. The merge() function is used to combine two maps into a single map in Terraform.

question: You have a SQL Database that's currently in production with live data. You need to change the database's pricing tier, but the change requires destroying and recreating the database. You want to ensure the new database is created before the old one is destroyed to avoid downtime. What should you add to your resource configuration?
questionPlain: You have a SQL Database that's currently in production with live data. You need to change the database's pricing tier, but the change requires destroying and recreating the database. You want to ensure the new database is created before the old one is destroyed to avoid downtime. What should you add to your resource configuration?

choices.text: add a lifecycle block with create_before_destroy = true
add a lifecycle block with prevent_destroy = true
add a depends_on argument pointing to the new database
add a count argument set to 2 to create both databases

explanation:
Objective 4f - Define resource dependencies in configuration

The lifecycle block with create_before_destroy = true changes Terraform's default behavior of destroying resources before creating replacements. When set to true, Terraform will create the new database first, then destroy the old one, minimizing downtime. This is particularly useful for stateful resources, such as databases, where you need service continuity during replacement operations.
feedbacks: Adding a lifecycle block with create_before_destroy = true ensures that the new database is created before the old one is destroyed. This helps avoid downtime by keeping the database available during the transition.

Adding a lifecycle block with prevent_destroy = true would prevent the database from being destroyed, which is not the desired behavior in this scenario, where the goal is to change the pricing tier by recreating the database. Adding a lifecycle block with create_before_destroy = true ensures that the new database is created before the old one is destroyed.

Adding a depends_on argument pointing to the new database would establish a dependency relationship between the resources, but it would not guarantee that the new database is created before the old one is destroyed. This approach may not prevent downtime during the transition. Adding a lifecycle block with create_before_destroy = true ensures that the new database is created before the old one is destroyed.

Adding a count argument set to 2 to create both databases would create two databases simultaneously, which is not necessary in this case where the goal is to replace the existing database with a new one without downtime. This approach would not ensure the desired sequence of creating the new database before destroying the old one. Adding a lifecycle block with create_before_destroy = true ensures that the new database is created before the old one is destroyed.

questionPlain: True or False? Terraform can only manage dependencies between resources if the depends_on argument is explicitly set for the dependent resources.

That means Terraform builds a dependency map (also known as a resource graph) to help determine which resources it can create in parallel and which resources are dependent on others, based on the interpolation used within the configuration.
feedbacks: While the depends_on argument can be used to explicitly set dependencies between resources in Terraform, it is not the only way to manage dependencies. Terraform also automatically detects implicit dependencies based on resource references in the configuration, allowing it to handle resource dependencies without the need for explicit depends_on declarations.

False. While the depends_on argument can be used to explicitly set dependencies between resources in Terraform, it is not the only way to manage dependencies. Terraform also automatically detects implicit dependencies based on resource references in the configuration, allowing it to handle resource dependencies without the need for explicit depends_on declarations.

question: You're deploying a GCP Compute Engine instance and want to verify that the instance receives a public IP address after creation. If it doesn't, you want Terraform to fail with an error. Which validation mechanism should you use?
questionPlain: You're deploying a GCP Compute Engine instance and want to verify that the instance receives a public IP address after creation. If it doesn't, you want Terraform to fail with an error. Which validation mechanism should you use?

choices.text: add a postcondition in the lifecycle block of the instance resource
add a precondition in the lifecycle block of the instance resource
add a validation block to the instance resource
add a check block that references the instance

explanation:
Objective 4g - Validate configuration using custom conditions

Postconditions are evaluated after a resource is created or updated and can verify that the resource was created with expected attributes. Since you need to check the instance's public IP after creation, a postcondition is appropriate. You would add it to the lifecycle block with a condition like self.network_interface[0].access_config[0].nat_ip != "". If the condition fails, Terraform will error and the operation fails, ensuring you don't proceed with infrastructure that doesn't meet your requirements.
feedbacks: Adding a postcondition in the lifecycle block of the instance resource allows you to verify the state of the resource after it has been created. In this case, you can check if the instance has received a public IP address, and if not, Terraform will fail with an error.

Adding a precondition in the lifecycle block of the instance resource would check the state of the resource before it is created. This is not suitable for verifying the public IP address of the instance after creation.

Adding a validation block to the instance resource is not a valid mechanism in Terraform for verifying the public IP address of the instance after creation. Validation blocks are used for input validation, not for checking the resource's state after creation.

While check blocks can enforce conditions across resources; the most appropriate mechanism here is a postcondition on the resource itself, because you want the resource’s own lifecycle to fail if it does not have a public IP after creation.

question: True or False? Marking an output as sensitive does not prevent its value from being stored in the Terraform state file.
questionPlain: True or False? Marking an output as sensitive does not prevent its value from being stored in the Terraform state file.

choices.text: True
False

explanation:
Objective 4h - Understand best practices for managing sensitive data, including secrets management with Vault

Use the sensitive argument on variable and output blocks when you want to redact those values from Terraform CLI log output and the HCP Terraform UI. Terraform also treats any expressions that reference a sensitive variable or output as inherently sensitive.
feedbacks: True. Marking an output as sensitive in Terraform only affects the display of the value in the CLI output and logs. It does not prevent the value from being stored in the Terraform state file, so it can still be accessed by anyone with access to the state file.

Incorrect. Marking an output as sensitive in Terraform does prevent its value from being displayed in the CLI output and logs, but it does not prevent the value from being stored in the Terraform state file. This means that the sensitive information can still be accessed by anyone with access to the state file.

question: Your team uses Vault for short-lived credentials and stores Terraform state in a remote backend. Which statements reflect best practices for managing sensitive data and state? (select four)
questionPlain: Your team uses Vault for short-lived credentials and stores Terraform state in a remote backend. Which statements reflect best practices for managing sensitive data and state? (select four)

choices.text: Terraform state can include sensitive data, so it is essential to restrict access to the state and audit any changes.
When using local state, the state file is stored in plain text by default
Using Vault ensures that secrets never appear in state, so additional controls on state aren’t required.
A properly configured remote backend improves security via encryption and access controls.
HCP Terraform encrypts state at rest (and in transit) and provides RBAC to restrict who can access state
Marking an output sensitive = true prevents its value from being stored in the state file.

explanation:
Objective 4h - Understand best practices for managing sensitive data, including secrets management with Vault

Terraform state can contain sensitive data, depending on the resources in use and your definition of "sensitive." The state contains resource IDs and all resource attributes. For resources such as databases, this may contain initial passwords.

When using local state, the state file is stored in plain-text JSON files.

If you manage any sensitive data with Terraform (like database passwords, user passwords, or private keys), treat the state itself as sensitive data.

Storing Terraform state remotely can provide better security.
feedbacks: Restricting access to Terraform state is crucial to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data. By auditing changes to the state, you can track who made modifications and when they were made, enhancing security and compliance.

Storing Terraform state in plain text when using local state is a security risk, as it exposes sensitive information. It is recommended to use a remote backend to store state securely and prevent unauthorized access.

While Vault helps manage secrets and prevents them from appearing in Terraform state, additional controls on state are still necessary to ensure comprehensive security measures are in place. Vault complements state management but does not eliminate the need for secure state handling.

Using a properly configured remote backend for storing Terraform state enhances security by encrypting the state data and providing access controls. This ensures that sensitive information is protected and only accessible to authorized users.

HCP Terraform encrypts state both at rest and in transit, adding an extra layer of security to protect sensitive data. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) further enhances security by restricting access to state files based on user roles and permissions.

Marking an output as sensitive = true does NOT prevent its value from being stored in the state file; it only prevents the value from being displayed in the terminal and logs. This is still a good practice to follow when dealing with confidential data in Terraform outputs.

question: You discovered a module on the Terraform Registry that will provision the resources you need. What other information can you find on the Terraform Registry to help you quickly use this module? (select three)
questionPlain: You discovered a module on the Terraform Registry that will provision the resources you need. What other information can you find on the Terraform Registry to help you quickly use this module? (select three)

choices.text: required input variables
a list of outputs
dependencies to use the module
a download button to quickly get the module code

explanation:
Objective 5a - Explain how Terraform sources modules

The Terraform Registry makes it simple to find and use modules.

Every page on the registry has a search field for finding modules. Enter any type of module you're looking for (examples: "vault," "vpc," "database"), and the resulting modules will be listed. The search query will look at the module name, provider, and description to match your search terms. On the results page, filters can be used to further refine search results.
feedbacks: Required input variables are essential information that you can find on the Terraform Registry for a module. Knowing the required input variables will help you understand what parameters need to be provided when using the module in your Terraform configuration.

A list of outputs is crucial information that you can find on the Terraform Registry for a module. Outputs define the values that the module will return after provisioning the resources, allowing you to access and use those values in other parts of your Terraform configuration.

Dependencies to use the module are important information that you can find on the Terraform Registry. Understanding the dependencies of a module will help you ensure that you have all the necessary components in place before using the module in your Terraform configuration.

While the Terraform Registry may have a download button to quickly get the module code, this is not one of the key pieces of information that will help you quickly use the module. The more critical information includes required input variables, a list of outputs, and dependencies to use the module effectively.

question:
You are reviewing the following Terraform configuration in main.tf. Which statements about this configuration are correct? (select two)


module "servers" {
  source  = "./modules/btk-cluster"
  servers = 5
}

choices.text: main.tf is the root (calling) module
btk-cluster refers to a local child module on disk
the argument servers must be declared as an output in the child module.
Terraform will download btk-cluster from the public registry when running terraform init

explanation:
Objective 5a - Explain how Terraform sources modules

To call a module means to include the contents of that module into the configuration with specific values for its input variables. Modules are called from within other modules using module blocks. A module that includes a module block like this is the calling module of the child module.

The label immediately after the module keyword is a local name, which the calling module can use to refer to this instance of the module.
feedbacks: main.tf is indeed the root module in this configuration, as it is the main entry point for the Terraform configuration. It is where the module servers block is defined, which calls the child module btk-cluster.

The source ./modules/btk-cluster indicates that btk-cluster is a local child module located in the modules directory relative to the root module. This allows the root module to reference and use the resources defined in the child module.

The argument servers in the module block is used to specify the number of servers to create in the child module. It does not necessarily need to be declared as an output in the child module, as it is being passed as a parameter to the child module for configuration.

Since the source ./modules/btk-cluster refers to a local child module on disk, Terraform will not download btk-cluster from the public registry when running terraform init. Instead, it will use the local module located in the specified directory.

question:
You have a root module that calls the child module modules/web. In modules/web/main.tf, a developer added name = "${var.env}-app".

What is the correct way to make this work?
questionPlain: You have a root module that calls the child module modules/web. In modules/web/main.tf, a developer added name = "${var.env}-app".What is the correct way to make this work?

choices.text: Declare variable "env" {} in the child module and pass it from root using env = var.env
Reference the parent directly: name = "${parent.var.env}-app" in the child module to read the value
Use the terraform workspace command in the child module to replace the need for var.env
Define locals { env = var.env } in the root module since child modules inherit locals automatically

explanation:
Objective 5b - Describe variable scope within modules

Variables are scoped to the current module. The child must declare variable "env" and the root must pass a value via the module block. No implicit inheritance or parent reference exists.
feedbacks: This is the correct way to make the variable env available in the child module. By declaring the variable env in the child module and passing it from the root module using env = var.env, the child module can access and use the value of env in its configuration.

Referencing the parent directly in the child module to read the value of var.env is not the correct approach. Child modules should receive variables from the root module explicitly to maintain modularity and reusability.

Using the terraform workspace command in the child module is not the correct way to make the variable env available. Workspaces are used to manage different environments or configurations, not to pass variables between modules.

Defining locals { env = var.env } in the root module is not the correct approach for making the variable env available in the child module. Locals are scoped to the module where they are defined and are not automatically inherited by child modules.

question:
A root module includes several variables in terraform.tfvars. You add a child module as shown below. What values can the child module access by default?


module "web" {
  source = "./modules/web"
}

choices.text: Only values passed to it via the module block since root variables are not automatically accessible inside the module.
All of the root variables from terraform.tfvars since children inherit parent variable values automatically.
Any root variables, as long as they are defined by a locals block, since locals are global across the configuration.
Only values that are defined as outputs in the root module since outputs are always available to children in the same run.

explanation:
Objective 5b - Describe variable scope within modules

Child modules have no implicit access to the parent’s variables, locals, or outputs. Pass inputs explicitly in the module block; outputs flow upward from child to parent, not the other way. Example where count and image are values that are being passed into the module and would be accessible by the child module.


module "web" {
  <module-specific-inputs>
  source = "./modules/web"

  count = var.num_vms
  image = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
}
feedbacks: By default, child modules in Terraform do not have access to root variables defined in terraform.tfvars. The child module needs to explicitly receive values through the module block to access specific variables from the root module.

Child modules do not inherit parent variable values automatically in Terraform. Each module operates independently and needs to receive values explicitly through the module block to access specific variables from the root module.

Locals in Terraform are scoped within the configuration where they are defined and are not global across the entire configuration. Child modules cannot access root variables defined in terraform.tfvars through locals blocks.
Outputs in Terraform are used to expose specific values from a module to be used by other parts of the configuration. Child modules cannot access these output values from the root module.
